description_full: A. O. Smith Corporation manufactures and markets residential and commercial gas and electric water heaters, boilers, heat pumps, tanks, and water treatment products in North America, China, Europe, and India. The company offers water heaters for residences, restaurants, hotels, office buildings, laundries, car washes, and small businesses; boilers for hospitals, schools, hotels, homes, apartments, and condominiums, and other large commercial buildings; and water treatment products comprising point-of-entry water softeners, well water solutions, and whole-home water filtration products, and point-of-use carbon and reverse osmosis products for residences, restaurants, hotels, and offices. It also provides commercial water treatment and filtration products; expansion tanks, commercial solar water heating systems, swimming pool and spa heaters, and related products and parts; and electric wall-hung, gas tankless, combi-boiler, and heat pump and solar water heaters. The company offers its products under the A. O. Smith, State, Lochinvar, Hague, Water-Right, Master Water, Atlantic Filter, Impact, and Water Tec brands. It distributes its products through independent wholesale plumbing distributors, as well as to retail channels consisting of hardware and home center chains, and manufacturer representative firms, as well as offers Aquasana branded products directly to consumers through e-commerce channels; and A. O. Smith branded water treatment products through dealer network and Amazon. A. O. Smith Corporation was founded in 1874 and is headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: A.O. Smith Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $8.6B market cap on $3.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 32% against a 9% cost of capital — a 24-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 38%.

The business throws off $546M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.13× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 54× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 6.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 10pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.71x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 11% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.86, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.04 vs 5y 0.83), so read it loosely.
About $81.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 28% in the 2020 crash, 42% in the 2022 bear market and 54% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $97.43, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 49%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $80.20 to $121 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 17.9 vs 24.1 and P/FCF 15.8 vs 22.9 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-2%).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $66.50 on average, 4% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 32% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 24pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.35).
It runs a 38% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.13x.
ROE of 29% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.5% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $38.2M (0% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.9, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.9 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.7% over 3 years, 5.8% over 5 years and 4.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 1.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 6.9% a year to shareholders (4.6% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 5.6% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 12.3% of the float, 6.7 days to cover.
people: With about 11,500 employees, each generates about $333K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 6.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $47K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.3M (7x revenue per employee).
